chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abi Basir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) pronounced the takbir (prayer of the deceased) over Hamzah seventy times, and Ali (peace be upon him) pronounced the takbir over Sahl ibn Hunayf twenty-five times.
He said: 'He pronounced the takbir in groups of five; whenever the people caught up with him, they would say,
O Commander of the Faithful, we have not caught up with the prayer over Sahl,
so he would lay him down and pronounce five takbirs over him, until he reached his grave, doing this five times.
The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And there is no prayer (of the deceased) among the Family of Muhammad for one who does not comprehend the prayer.

key_terms.آلُ مُحَمَّدٍ: The Family of Muhammad, referring to the Ahl al-Bayt.
key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful, a title primarily referring to Imam Ali.
key_terms.تَكْبِيرَة: Takbir (pronouncing 'Allahu Akbar'), a key component of the funeral prayer in Shia jurisprudence.
key_terms.صَلَاةُ الْجَنَازَةِ: Funeral prayer, the ritual prayer performed over a deceased Muslim.
key_terms.يَعْقِلُ الصَّلَاةَ: To comprehend/understand the prayer, referring to the mental presence and understanding of the ritual.

ai.seo_question: What is the number of takbirs pronounced over the deceased in Shia funeral prayers according to the practices of the Prophet and Imam Ali?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the Sunnah of variable takbir counts in funeral prayers, contrasting the Prophet’s seventy takbirs for Hamzah with Imam Ali’s twenty-five for Sahl ibn Hunayf, demonstrating the flexibility of ritual practice based on the deceased's status. The Sheikh al-Tusi’s concluding note clarifies that 'not praying' refers to the absence of the specific ritual prayer for those lacking religious comprehension, rather than a total denial of their merit. This distinction underscores the Shia emphasis on the intellectual and spiritual readiness of the deceased as a criterion for the full performance of funeral rites.
